newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-CALLS FOR COACH DU PLESSIS TO BE SACKED.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-CALLS FOR COACH DU PLESSIS TO BE SACKED.

text.p: Springbok coach Carel du Plessis bore the brunt of national anger on Sunday following South Africa's series defeat by the unheralded British Lions.
"Springbok Crisis" trumpeted the Sunday Independent, while the front page of the South African Sunday Times asked readers to ring in and vote whether du Plessis should be fired.
It was a tactic the same paper used last September when former coach Andre Markgraaff left Franois Pienaar out of his Springbok squad.
Pienaar, who writes a column for the London Sunday Telegraph, was quoted by the Sunday Times as being "heartbroken" by the Springbok performance.
Meanwhile the paper's main rugby writer, Dan Retief, layed the blame squarely at the feet of French referee Didier Mene, who he called "the man of Mene penalties".
Retief wrote, "a succession of unforgiveable errors by Mene, who had a mistake ridden afternoon, cruelly conspired to make the Boks pay for their own appalling goal-kicking".

Andy Irvine, one of the stars of the victorious 1974 Lions team said: "The South African goal kickers were terrible and should be shot. Carel du Plessis should know that you cannot go into a test match without a reliable goal kicker."

Former Springbok goal-kicking great Naas Botha said on television: "The Lions did not win the game, we lost it. They proved that even if you play badly, but have a reliable kicker, you are always in with a shout."

The omission of World Cup centre Hennie le Roux in favour of raw youngsters Percy Montogomery and Danie van Schalkwyk has been treated as a national disgrace not far below the non-selection of Pienaar last year.

The Johannesburg Star quotes le Roux's coach at Rand Afrikans University, Dr Thys Herbst. "I don't know where the stories come from regarding Hennie telling Carel he is not ready to play for South Africa. The way I see it, it's all just politics. Carel was definitely under pressure not to select Hennie, I'm certain of that."
The is speculation in the press that South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) president Louis Luyt was behind the black-balling of le Roux.

The Independent also said that Luyt refused to take part in the ceremony handing back the William Webb Ellis Trophy to the Lions at Newlands last week because he could not face being booed by the capacity crowd. He instead passed the buck to his vice-president, Mluleki George.

The only voice of apparent reason came from British writer Nick Cain who wrote in the Independent: "Such was the savagery of the (South African) media beating that it left even hardened British hacks wincing."
Cain and his colleagues were taken aback at the importance attached to the game in this country and told a story about the East London Daily Dispatch newspaper.

"For the Lions second match against Border the front-page headline was 'Lions Match-Worry Over Waterlogged Pitch', while at the bottom of the page there was room for a much smaller story, 'Mandela Assassination Threat Uncovered'."
